meta.title: Modeling Reasoning — Catalogue Management
meta.description:
# Modeling Reasoning — Catalogue Management

## Scope
This chapter covers the Library Catalogue System from the project brief: maintaining catalogue entries (**BookTitle**, identity `titleId`: title, author, ISBN, genre, publication year, cover image) and their physical copies (**Copy**, identity `copyId`, references `titleId`, carrying its own availability lifecycle: available / reserved / checked-out / in-repair / lost). Two human roles (Librarian, Member) and one external system actor (Reservation and Pickup System) make up the Role Catalog.

## Assumptions added beyond the literal brief
- **Reservation status sync**: the brief's "Interfaces to Other Teams" section only explicitly names borrowed/returned/lost as incoming updates, but the catalogue's own three-way status vocabulary (available/reserved/checked-out) requires reservation placement and release to also cross in as external triggers. Modeled `ReservationPlaced` and `ReservationReleased` as additional external events for this reason.
- **CopyReturnedFromRepair**: added so "sent for repair" isn't a one-way trap door — not in the literal brief, but required for the catalogue to stay usable.
- **CopyReportedLost has no recovery path** (deliberately *not* added, unlike repair): flagged as an open QUESTION comment on the `CopyReportedLost` node rather than silently added or silently omitted — accepted debt pending confirmation this scenario matters to the business.

## Business rules encoded as scenarios, not new events
All copy/title state preconditions are enforced as Step 7 scenario rejections, not as additional events: archived titles reject `AddCopy`/`UpdateBookTitleDetails`; `ArchiveBookTitle` itself rejects while any copy is still checked out; each copy-status command (`SendCopyForRepair`, `ReportCopyLost`, `ReserveCopy`, `CheckOutCopy`, `ReturnCopy`, `ReleaseCopyReservation`) rejects when the copy isn't in the one prerequisite state that action requires. None of these needed a dedicated event — they're validation outcomes, not new domain facts.

## Sequencing / design corrections made mid-workflow
The biggest correction: Step 5's first attempt placed `TitleDetailsView` and `CopyStatusListView` as single early instances meant to serve every consuming screen across the whole timeline via forward edges. This failed structural validation (9 backward-arrow rejections) because `BookTitleDetailsUpdated` and the copy-lifecycle events occur in columns *after* where the read models sat. Fixed by applying the "new copy of the read model" pattern for real: **TitleDetailsView has 2 progressively-scoped instances** (an early one sourcing only `BookTitleAdded`, feeding AddCopy/Edit-Details; a later one adding `BookTitleDetailsUpdated`, feeding only the Archive screen) and **CopyStatusListView has 3** (each adding one more copy-lifecycle event than the last, feeding SendCopyForRepair → RecordCopyReturnedFromRepair → ReportCopyLost in turn). This is why the same read-model title appears on multiple slices — each instance is a genuinely separate node with a narrower, causally-valid set of connected events, not a naming accident.

Also corrected along the way: `BookTitleDetailsUpdated` originally carried only a `changedFields` list with no actual new values — patched to carry the real updated field values, since no read model could otherwise project an edit.

## Read model design rationale
- **TitleDetailsView (Librarian) vs. CatalogueEntryView (Member)** are deliberately two different read models over overlapping source events, not one shared node — different audiences, different field sets (Librarian's is richer: ISBN, publication year; Member's is browse-optimized), different cardinality (Single vs. List). Conflating them would couple the Librarian's admin UI to the Member's catalogue UI for no reason.
- **CopyStatusListView and CatalogueEntryAvailabilityView/AvailableCopiesCountView are legitimate wide-fan-in roll-ups** (5-8 connected copy-lifecycle events each) — the >3-events heuristic's documented exception applies because each is a single homogeneous field (a copy's live status, or a per-title/library-wide availability count) that is by construction derived across a copy's whole lifecycle. None of these nodes bundle a narrow identity/fact field alongside the wide field — the antipattern the heuristic actually guards against.
- **CatalogueEntryView and CatalogueEntryAvailabilityView are each reused by two screens** (Catalogue Browse and Book Details) rather than duplicated — same query, same audience, Book Details is just filtered to one row.

## Cross-context integration
The **Reservation and Pickup System** is modeled as a second swimlane, out-of-scope external system (Conway's Law, Step 6) whose 4 events (`ReservationPlaced`, `BookCheckedOut`, `BookReturned`, `ReservationReleased`) each cross in via a **two-stage translation chain** (Step 4b): a translation automation mirrors the external event 1:1 into an internal event of the same name (no business logic, never closes its own todo list), then a separate worker automation reacts to that internal event and performs the actual domain decision (validating the copy's current state before accepting the transition), producing the chapter's own final domain event. This two-automation split is mandatory per the framework's rule that a worker automation can never be triggered directly by another system's event.

## Closing summary
15 events (11 own-domain + 4 external triggers, plus 4 mirrored internal translation events), 15 commands (7 Librarian + 8 automation-issued), 8 automations (4 translation + 4 worker), 18 read models (8 todo-lists + 10 screen-facing), 9 HTML screens (5 base +... multiple command-screen copies), 40 columns, 33 slice definitions. `validate_model` — **PASS**, 0 errors, 0 warnings throughout Steps 7–10. One open QUESTION comment (lost-copy recovery) is the only unresolved item, by design.
